messages.subject: resolving negative residual variances
parts:
Hi all,

I am running a multi-group unidimensional CFA to evaluate measurement invariance across gender groups on a 4 item scale with 4 point Likert type responses. Sample sizes in each group are n = 140 and n = 360 in the focal and reference groups, respectively. When I run a multigroup CFA using robust estimators (WLSMV, MLR, or MLM), I keep getting a model with one indicator with negative residual variance but this does not occur when I use ML estimation. I'm wondering if, despite the fact that the data are ordinal, it would be okay to use ML estimation in this case?

Any thoughts are appreciated!

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: resolving negative residual variances
parts: I keep getting a model with one indicator with negative residual variance but this does not occur when I use ML estimation. I'm wondering if, despite the fact that the data are ordinal, it would be okay to use ML estimation in this case?

No, your estimates would be substantially biased toward zero, underestimating the true reliability of your indicators.

http://psychmodels.ucdavis.edu/uploads/8/6/3/9/86398102/rhemtullabrosseauliardsavalei_pm.pdf

By implication, you would have diminished power to detect violations of invariance, because all the factor loadings would be biased toward zero; thus, any true differences would be estimated as smaller than they really are.  

This also probably accounts for why ML does not show a negative residual variance -- if loadings are smaller, then residual variances are larger.

A negative residual variance estimate is actually quite likely to occur when your N is small (this isn't really a small N for ML, but it is for DWLS: https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2014.859510), just because of sampling error.  So if your model fits approximately well and the 95% CI for the residual variance includes positive values, then sampling variability is probably the explanation for the Heywood case.  In other words, it is not a problem that needs fixing.

summary(fit, ci = TRUE)
